items: Evidence Documentation: Create a three-column scope audit worksheet listing every contracted item, its completion status, and supporting evidence like dated photos or communications.
Evidence Documentation: Photograph and video every defect on the property, capturing timestamps and visual context that document substandard work and unfinished areas.
Evidence Documentation: Organize all change orders in a separate section noting whether they were signed by both parties, their agreed costs, and their current completion status.
Evidence Documentation: Record the first date you noticed each problem, establishing a timeline that shows the contractor's awareness of defects before they were addressed.
Financial Controls: Stop all further payments to the contractor immediately and place any pending checks on hold until you complete your full scope audit.
Financial Controls: File a stop-payment notice with your county recorder within 10 days of each payment to alert subcontractors and protect your lien rights.
Financial Controls: Issue a written scope freeze that defines exactly which original contracted items must be completed before any new work begins.
Financial Controls: Calculate your total financial exposure by compiling every payment made, all outstanding invoices, and projected costs to finish remaining work.
Legal Leverage: Send a certified letter documenting the contractor's failures, your documented discrepancies, and a specific deadline for resolution to create a formal record.
Legal Leverage: Research your state's preliminary lien notice requirements and file one immediately to establish priority over other claimants against your property.
Legal Leverage: Document every delay caused by this contractor that negatively affected other trades, recording specific dates and back charge amounts where applicable.
Legal Leverage: Consult a construction attorney within one week to understand which legal mechanisms like stop-payment notices and back charges apply to your situation.
